title: Chapter 125 — The Log and Line
paragraphs: Though the fated Pequod had now been afloat so long on this voyage, the log and line — a wooden float paid out astern from a reel on a line, to measure the ship's speed — had very seldom been used. Owing to a confident reliance on other means of determining the vessel's position, some merchantmen, and many whalemen, especially when cruising, wholly neglect to heave the log; though at the same time, and often more for form's sake than anything else, they regularly put down on the customary slate the course steered by the ship, as well as the presumed average rate of progress every hour. It had been so with the Pequod. The wooden reel and the angular log attached to it hung, long untouched, just beneath the railing of the after bulwarks. Rain and spray had dampened it; sun and wind had warped it; all the elements had combined to rot a thing that hung so idly. But, heedless of all this, his mood seized Ahab as he happened to glance at the reel, not many hours after the magnet scene; and he remembered that his quadrant was no more, and recalled his frantic oath about the level log and line. The ship was sailing with a plunging motion; astern, the billows rolled in riots.
"Forward, there! Heave the log!"
Two seamen came. The golden-hued Tahitian and the grizzled Manxman. "Take the reel, one of you; I'll heave."
They went toward the far end of the stern, on the ship's lee side, where the deck, tilted by the slanting force of the wind, was now almost dipping into the creamy sea that rushed past alongside.

The Manxman took the reel and held it up high by the handles sticking out at each end of the spindle on which the spool of line turned; he stood like that, with the angular log hanging down, until Ahab came up to him.

Ahab stood in front of him and was lightly unwinding some thirty or forty turns to make a preliminary hand-coil for tossing overboard, when the old Manxman, who was watching both him and the line intently, ventured to speak.
"Sir, I mistrust it; this line looks far gone. Long heat and wet have spoiled it."
"It will hold, old gentleman. Long heat and wet — have they spoiled you? You seem to hold. Or, truer perhaps, life holds you; not you it."
"I hold the spool, sir. But just as my captain says. With these gray hairs of mine, it's not worth while disputing, especially with a superior who'll never confess."
"What's that? There now's a patched professor in Queen Nature's granite-founded College; but I think he's too subservient. Where were you born?"
"In the little rocky Isle of Man, sir."
"Excellent! You've hit the world by that."
"I don't know, sir, but I was born there."

"In the Isle of Man, eh? Well, taken the other way, it's good. Here's a man from Man; a man born in once-independent Man, and now unmanned of Man; which is sucked in — by what? Up with the reel! In the end the dead, blind wall butts every questioning head. Up with it! There."

The log was heaved. The loose coils rapidly straightened out in a long dragging line astern, and then instantly the reel began to whirl. In turn, as the log was jerkingly raised and lowered by the rolling waves, its towing resistance caused the old reelman to stagger strangely.
"Hold hard!"
Snap! The line, strained too far, sagged down in a single long loop; the tugging log was gone.

"I smash the quadrant, the thunder reverses the needles, and now the mad sea snaps the log-line. But Ahab can mend everything. Haul in here, Tahitian; reel up, Manxman. And listen: get the carpenter to make another log, and you mend the line. See to it."

"There he goes now; to him nothing has happened; but to me it feels as if the skewer is working loose from the middle of the world. Haul in, haul in, Tahitian! These lines go out whole and whirling, and come back broken and dragging slow. Ha, Pip? Come to help, eh, Pip?"

"Pip? Who are you calling Pip? Pip jumped from the whale-boat. Pip's missing. Let's see now if you haven't fished him up here, fisherman. It drags hard; I guess he's holding on. Jerk him, Tahiti! Jerk him off; we haul in no cowards here. Ho! There's his arm just breaking water. A hatchet! A hatchet! Cut it off — we haul in no cowards here. Captain Ahab! Sir, sir! Here's Pip, trying to get on board again."
"Peace, you crazy loon," cried the Manxman, seizing him by the arm. "Away from the quarter-deck!"
"The greater idiot always scolds the lesser," muttered Ahab, advancing. "Hands off that holiness! Where did you say Pip was, boy?"
"Astern there, sir, astern! Look! Look!"
"And who are you, boy? I don't see my reflection in the vacant pupils of your eyes. Oh God! That man should be a thing for immortal souls to sieve through! Who are you, boy?"

"Bell-boy, sir; ship's crier; ding, dong, ding! Pip! Pip! Pip! One hundred pounds of clay reward for Pip; five feet high — looks cowardly — quickest known by that! Ding, dong, ding! Who's seen Pip the coward?"

"There can be no hearts above the snow-line. Oh, you frozen heavens! Look down here. You begot this luckless child, and have abandoned him, you creative libertines. Here, boy; Ahab's cabin shall be Pip's home henceforth, while Ahab lives. You touch my inmost center, boy; you are tied to me by cords woven of my heart-strings. Come, let's go down."

"What's this? Here's velvet shark-skin," gazing intently at Ahab's hand and feeling it. "Ah, now, if poor Pip had only felt so kind a thing as this, maybe he'd never have been lost! This seems to me, sir, like a man-rope, something weak souls can hold on to. Oh, sir, let old Perth come now and rivet these two hands together, the black one with the white, for I won't let this go."

"Oh, boy, nor will I let go of you, unless by holding on I should drag you to worse horrors than are here. Come, then, to my cabin. Look, you believers in gods all goodness and in man all ill — look, you! See the omniscient gods oblivious of suffering man; and man, though idiotic and not knowing what he does, yet full of the sweet things of love and gratitude. Come! I feel prouder leading you by your black hand than if I grasped an Emperor's!"

"There go two daft ones now," muttered the old Manxman. "One daft with strength, the other daft with weakness. But here's the end of the rotten line — all dripping, too. Mend it, eh? I think we had best have a new line altogether. I'll see Mr. Stubb about it."
